item.title: China marks start of war against Japanese aggression, preserving living memories
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
* Friday marked the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, the start of China's 14-year war of resistance against Japanese aggression. On Sept. 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of railway near Shenyang under their control and accused Chinese troops of sabotage, using this as a pretext for their later attack that night on barracks near Shenyang, thus launching their premeditated invasion of China. * The commemorations in Shenyang anchored nationwide events marking the 95th anniversary of the incident. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) broke out first and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded. * Meanwhile, a nationwide effort is ongoing as China seeks to preserve memories of the War of Resistance, forming a multi-layered system that spans from top-level government planning to grassroots participation. SHENYANG, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Air-raid sirens wailed. Traffic halted. Pedestrians stood still. At 9:18 a.m. on Friday, the city of Shenyang in northeast China's Liaoning Province paused for a three-minute silence to mourn those killed in the Japanese invasion of China and to cherish hard-won peace. Friday marked the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, the start of China's 14-year war of resistance against Japanese aggression. On Sept. 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of railway near Shenyang under their control and accused Chinese troops of sabotage, using this as a pretext for their later attack that night on barracks near Shenyang, thus launching their premeditated invasion of China. Since 1995, Shenyang has sounded air-raid sirens annually on this day to commemorate the incident. "Those few minutes when everything stopped for the sirens reminded me that our everyday life is built on hard-won peace," said Li Xuyang, an employee of Brilliance Auto based in Shenyang. The commemorations in Shenyang anchored nationwide events marking the 95th anniversary of the incident. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) broke out first and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded. LEST WE FORGET At a ceremony held on Friday morning at the 9.18 Historical Museum, which was built near the site of the railway explosion, 14 representatives from all walks of life solemnly tolled the Bell of Warning. The 14 chimes echoed through the air, symbolizing the 14 arduous years of the Chinese people's fight against Japanese invaders. Li Hongzhong, vice chairman of the National People's Congress Standing Committee and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, attended the ceremony and delivered a speech. The War of Resistance marked China's first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times, Li said. He called for drawing lessons from history to light the way forward, stressing the importance of upholding the Party's overall leadership, advancing Chinese modernization, and contributing to building a community with a shared future for humanity. "I learned about the September 18 Incident in textbooks. Hearing the bell today, I want to know even more about what children of my age went through back then," said Ma Zihao, a sixth grader in Shenyang. "Seeing today's children able to go to school without a worry makes me feel that the sacrifices back then were not in vain," said Yang Huafeng, a 93-year-old veteran of the war who attended the event. "I hope they remember the martyrs who laid down their lives for this country and understand how precious peace is." An exhibition of irrefutable evidence of Japan's invasion of northeast China also opened on Friday at the 9.18 Historical Museum. The exhibition features more than 300 historical photographs and archival documents, along with over 100 physical artifacts, including original archives, newspapers and pictorials, banknotes, stamps, and investigation reports. "The annual observances give the younger generation a chance to rethink the relationship between war and their own lives. Only by remembering the suffering war brought to ordinary people can we truly appreciate how precious peace is and what it takes to protect it," said Gao Jian, a researcher at the museum. A similar bell-tolling ceremony was held on Friday at the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders in Nanjing, capital of east China's Jiangsu Province. At this event, university students recited poetry honoring the Chinese people's unyielding spirit of resistance. For Zhang Boxiang, a student at Nanjing University of the Arts, one line stood out: "The fate of our nation must now be decided by ourselves." "Standing on the memorial square and speaking those words felt like responding to peers from over 80 years ago," he said. "They had no way out. We today must never forget." On Dec. 13, 1937, Japanese troops captured the then-Chinese capital Nanjing, unleashing six weeks of devastation that claimed the lives of an estimated 300,000 civilians and unarmed soldiers. In late August this year, the 9.18 Historical Museum was officially designated a patriotism education base by the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League (TDSL). It is the seventh such base established by the TDSL Central Committee. The designation reaffirms the inseparable historical role of Taiwan compatriots in the nationwide resistance against Japanese aggression and highlights the shared history of people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, who fought together against foreign aggression and belong to one Chinese nation. "Countless patriots and martyrs sacrificed their lives for the recovery of Taiwan -- a vivid testament to the unyielding spirit of the Chinese nation's resistance," Qiu Zhibin, grandnephew of veteran Taiwan patriot Qiu Niantai, said at the event. He called on people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to remember their shared history, carry forward that spirit, and join hands in advancing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. KEEPING MEMORIES ALIVE Meanwhile, a nationwide effort is ongoing as China seeks to preserve memories of the War of Resistance, forming a multi-layered system that spans from top-level government planning to grassroots participation. According to the National Cultural Heritage Administration, China has completed a comprehensive survey of its wartime heritage. As of last year, the country had more than 10,000 immovable and over 500,000 movable cultural relics related to the War of Resistance. From 2021 to 2025, nearly 20 wartime memorial halls were renovated or expanded, bringing the total number of registered wartime memorial halls to 257. Yet the most urgent task remains collecting oral histories from those with firsthand experience of the War of Resistance, which is a race against time. Over the past three decades, Jin Chengmin, a senior researcher at the Exhibition Hall of Evidence of Crimes Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army in Harbin, capital of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, and his team have conducted more than 40 cross-border investigations. They traveled to countries including Japan, the United States and Russia, interviewing over 80 former Unit 731 members and collecting 423 hours of testimony. This testimony, together with almost 300,000 archival items, more than 20,000 artifacts, 22 hours of audio recordings from the Khabarovsk trial and 27 existing sites, forms a complete chain of evidence documenting Japan's bacterial warfare crimes. "History cannot be buried, and peace is not for trade. This is our bottom line and our faith. The evidence of Unit 731's crimes does not belong to China alone. It is a wound shared by all humanity," Jin said. "What we can do is keep our research rigorous and bring the truth to light, so that more people see it, remember it and stay alert." According to Zhang Lianhong, a professor at Nanjing Normal University, the university, in collaboration with other universities and volunteer organizations, earlier this year completed a major national research project on preserving the oral histories of veterans who fought in the War of Resistance. The 10-year project involved nearly 1,000 teachers, students and volunteers, who sought out 1,442 veterans with an average age of 95, producing over 10 million words in transcripts and more than 3,000 hours of video interviews. "Ten years ago, the veterans were already in their twilight years, passing away one after another, with only tens of thousands still alive," said Zhang, who has long studied the history of the War of Resistance and the Nanjing Massacre. "As historians, we are duty-bound to seize the last chance to record their stories." Grassroots efforts are also stepping up. Based in Qinxian County, north China's Shanxi Province, 81-year-old Li Guoqing spent over a decade traveling by motorcycle across 12 provincial-level regions, covering more than 100,000 kilometers. He located 595 witnesses to over 400 cases of Japanese wartime atrocities and recorded numerous oral histories with his own camera. But keeping memories alive takes more than preservation. It also means passing them on. From 2021 to 2025, an average of more than 500 exhibitions on the War of Resistance were held nationwide each year, with over 60 million visits recorded at wartime sites and memorial halls. The rise of digital technology and new media is also giving the public new ways to engage with wartime history. In June, a red archive knowledge base jointly built by Sichuan Archives and multiple partners went online, with its first phase in 2025 focusing on archives of the War of Resistance. By April, China's first AI agent for archival exhibitions, developed on this knowledge base, had served almost 10,000 visitors at the archives' offline exhibitions. Even at his advanced age, Li Guoqing is still working to master new technologies. He spent 6,000 yuan (about 889 U.S. dollars) to learn how to produce and share short videos, turning witnesses' stories into oral history clips. More than 130 episodes have been posted online, with the series expected to reach 500 episodes. "I need to hurry. I'm already in my 80s," he said. "I hope I can finish this series in my lifetime and do my part to preserve the memory of the War of Resistance." (Reporting by Cui Enhui, Yao Yuan, Cui Shihao, Zhao Hongnan, Qiu Bingqing, Yang Siqi, Xu Kaixin and He Shan; Video reporters: Yang Qing, Ma Haoran, Jiang Zhaochen, Liu Bin, Zhao Yong and Gao Ming; Video editors: Zhou Yang, Wu You and Li Qin) ■

item.title: U.S. returns 64 cultural relics, fossils to China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Chinese staff members prepare to pack a cultural relic in New York, the United States, Sept. 17, 2026. The United States has returned 64 Chinese cultural relics and paleontological fossils to China, China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) said Thursday. The items were handed over in two batches in Washington and New York on Wednesday and Thursday by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, respectively. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo) NEW YORK, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The United States has returned 64 Chinese cultural relics and paleontological fossils to China, China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) said Thursday. The items were handed over in two batches in Washington and New York on Wednesday and Thursday by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, respectively. At the return ceremonies, Rao Quan, vice minister of Culture and Tourism and administrator of the NCHA, signed the confirmation of the return and receipt on behalf of the Chinese side. The returned items, seized by U.S. law enforcement agencies, include the torso of a bodhisattva statue from the Tianlongshan Grottoes, as well as statues, terracotta figures, dinosaur skeleton fossils, fish fossils and dinosaur egg fossils. The NCHA said that it worked with Chinese diplomatic and consular missions in the United States and relevant U.S. authorities to facilitate the return of the artifacts and that this week's return marked the fifth time the Manhattan District Attorney's Office had returned cultural relics to China. The latest repatriations are part of China-U.S. cooperation to combat illicit trafficking of Chinese cultural property under a memorandum of understanding signed in 2009 and renewed three times since. Present at the ceremonies were Chinese Ambassador to the United States Xie Feng and Consul General in New York Chen Li, along with representatives from the U.S. State Department, the HSI and the Manhattan District Attorney's Office. ■ Rao Quan (2nd R), vice minister of Culture and Tourism and administrator of China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, signs the confirmation of the return and receipt of Chinese cultural property with a U.S. representative in Washington, D.C., the United States, Sept. 16, 2026. item.title: Along the Long March route, remembrance endures amid change
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
NANNING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Every so often, Jiang Shilin leaves his home in a village in south China and walks about 10 minutes up a mountain path to visit a grave. The 82-year-old has made the journey for as long as he can remember. Sometimes he carries a sickle to clear away the weeds. Other times, he brings a brush and paint to retrace the fading characters on the gravestone. Seven people are buried there. Jiang never knew them. He does not even know their names. But he knows how they died. REMEMBRANCE More than 90 years ago, the hills around Caiwan Village in Quanzhou County, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, became a battlefield. The seven were soldiers of the Red Army, the armed forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC). They were taking part in the Long March, a 1934-1936 military maneuver that helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the CPC. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and vast grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers -- a trek later described by American journalist Harrison Salisbury as "a great human epic." In the winter of 1934 during the Long March, the Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the Kuomintang troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle. For families such as Jiang's, however, memories of the Red Army were shaped not only by the fighting, but also by their encounters with the soldiers. Jiang grew up hearing stories of those days from his father. "My father told us that when the Red Army came to the village, the soldiers helped villagers carry water and do chores. The villagers, in turn, showed them the way, cooked sweet potatoes for them and brought them water," Jiang said. Not long after the Red Army moved on, Jiang's grandfather, Jiang Zhongtai, and Jiang's father found the bodies of seven soldiers while collecting firewood on a nearby hill. They buried the bodies where they found them and marked the site with three small bricks. Before Jiang Zhongtai died, he left his son with a request: Don't forget the grave. For over nine decades, the family has kept that promise. As a boy, Jiang would follow his father up the hill before festivals. He once asked why they returned year after year to honor men whose names they did not even know. "My father said the Red Army fought for ordinary people," Jiang recalled. "We may not know who these men were, but we must not forget them." Traces of the Battle of the Xiangjiang River can still be found along the river and in the surrounding hills. Old ferry crossings remain, along with graves of fallen Red Army soldiers. Some bear names. Others do not. Jiang's family is not alone in caring for them. In nearby Xing'an County, generations of Li Guida's family have tended the graves of 12 Red Army soldiers. Li, an ethnic Yao villager, said his grandfather once guided Red Army troops through the area. After the fighting, he joined other villagers in recovering and burying fallen soldiers under the cover of darkness. "My grandfather used to say that the Red Army helped farmers have enough to eat, so we should always remember what they did for us," Li said. Similar memories of the ties between Red Army soldiers and local residents have been passed down elsewhere along the route of the Long March. In Rucheng, central China's Hunan Province, three female soldiers are remembered for sharing their only quilt with a villager who had given them shelter. Before leaving, they cut the quilt in two and left half behind. CHANGE In Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, rugged terrain and poor transport links long constrained local development. Today, roads wind through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, connecting once-isolated villages with the outside world. Economic development accelerated in the decades after China launched its reform and opening-up drive in the late 1970s. By 2020, more than 100 impoverished villages across the three counties had been lifted out of poverty following years of targeted poverty alleviation efforts. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March and the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan calls for developing county economies with distinctive local strengths and fostering counties that excel in agriculture, industry or tourism. Today, the three counties are developing specialty agriculture, rural tourism and traditional industries as part of their rural revitalization efforts. Citrus farming, for example, has become an important source of income in Xing'an, where more than 40,000 farming households benefit from citrus exports. The citrus industry there generates over 1.1 billion yuan (163 million U.S. dollars) in annual output. Near the Xiangjiang River, Guilin Jolly Cool Fruit Agricultural Products Co., Ltd. ships locally grown mandarins to markets in Central and Southeast Asia. Some local farming households now earn 50,000 to 60,000 yuan a year from growing the fruit and working at the company's factory. "Our goal is not simply to sell the fruit, but to make sure more local people benefit from the industry," said Sun Kai, a sales manager at the company. The area's wartime history has also become a resource for tourism and local development. Not far from a memorial hall dedicated to the Battle of the Xiangjiang River in Quanzhou County, entrepreneur You Wei runs a study tour center that receives about 40,000 students a year. Through activities such as learning battlefield first aid, making stretchers and transporting supplies, students gain a better understanding of what happened there more than nine decades ago. "The hardships endured by the Red Army on the Long March helped pave the way for the better lives we have today," You said. "We hope young people can also learn from their courage and draw strength from it when facing challenges of their own." The changes are visible within Jiang's own family. His father attended night school after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, while the family's thatched home was eventually replaced by the two-story house where Jiang lives today. One of his granddaughters now works at a company in design and cost estimation; another is in high school and hopes to study in Beijing and pursue a career in technology. Jiang himself has traveled across much of China and visited Vietnam, Singapore and Malaysia. Yet one journey has remained unchanged. Around traditional festivals, Jiang still walks up the familiar mountain path, bringing offerings such as liquor, candies, biscuits, zongzi (sticky rice dumplings), and mooncakes. When fruit from the family's trees ripens, he brings plums, loquats or peaches. These days, his children and grandchildren sometimes make the walk with him. At the grave, they bow three times. "Thank you," Jiang silently told them. "You gave us the life we have today." ■

item.title: Intelligent connected NEVs set to boost China's auto industry upgrade
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The intelligent connected new energy vehicle (NEV) industry is anticipated to contribute greatly to the upgrading of China's automobile industry, along with continuous breakthroughs in core technologies in this sector amid the artificial intelligence boom. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and eight other departments in early September jointly released a plan for the development of the intelligent connected NEV industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan proposes that, by 2030, China will further consolidate its advantages across the entire intelligent connected NEV industrial chain and join the ranks of the world's auto powerhouses. Intelligent connected NEVs are the main direction for transforming and upgrading the country's automobile industry, are typical examples of new quality productive forces, and are key components in building a modern industrial system in China, the plan notes. This move is valued as a future-oriented strategic layout for strengthening the automobile industry which has undergone decades of constant progress in scale and core technologies and brands, with technological capabilities acting as the major driving power. In 2025, China's automobile production and sales respectively reached 34.53 million and 34.4 million units, up 10.4 percent and 9.4 percent year on year respectively. The industry has maintained over 30 million units for three consecutive years and ranked the first globally for 17 successive years. Of the total, production and sales of NEVs respectively reached nearly 16.63 million and 16.49 million units, ranking the first in the world for 11 years straight. The large-scale deployment of intelligent connected vehicle technology, notably, is reshaping the core competitiveness of China's automotive industry. In the first three quarters of 2025, 64 percent of new passenger vehicles in China were equipped with Level 2 (L2) combined driver-assistance functions. In 2026, this rate has climbed to 70 percent, and more than 30 percent of automobile models provide navigation-assisted driving functions. What's more significant, Level 3 (L3) conditional autonomous driving has run beyond closed-road testing into commercial application. It means China's industrialization of intelligent connected vehicle sector is accelerating on all fronts, including such major shift from technical validation to commercial deployment. Continuous breakthroughs in key technologies are generating strong momentum for auto industry upgrading. Major advances have been made in diverse areas such as batteries, charging, automotive chips and intelligent driving systems. More importantly, some of these innovative technologies have achieved large-scale commercial application in the Chinese auto market through rapid iterative innovation. China has developed an automotive technology ecosystem sustained by emerging technologies, innovative development models and novel business models, which lay a solid technological foundation for the country to achieve its goal of becoming one of the world's auto powerhouses. Looking ahead, the plan notes that by 2030, in the domestic market, new energy passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles will account for 70 percent and 40 percent respectively. Also, vehicles equipped with autonomous driving functions will be applied on a large scale. By 2030, key auto technologies will be significantly improved, with average fuel consumption of passenger vehicles reaching 3.3 liters per 100 km, and average electricity consumption of all-electric passenger vehicles reaching approximately 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 100 km. Highly automated driving will be achieved in scenarios like expressways, urban express roads and other urban roads, according to the plan. The plan points out that enhancing technological innovation capability is a key priority in intelligent connected NEV development. With critical areas focused on energy and power systems, intelligent chassis and intelligent connectivity, China will carry out strategic, forward-looking and pioneering R&D initiatives to drive the development of the next-generation technologies for intelligent connected NEVs. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, efforts will be made to uphold the bottom line of product quality and improve the safety and reliability of autonomous driving, said Xin Guobin, vice minister of the MIIT, at a recent media conference. Policies concerning NEV insurance will also be optimized, while maintenance costs will be reduced to address consumer concerns and encourage consumers to purchase and use NEVs with confidence, he added. ■

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: History warns against Japan's return to militarism
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Remembering the September 18 Incident today is not about perpetuating hatred. It is about understanding how militarism once led Japan down the path of aggression, and why any sign of that path being revisited deserves vigilance. BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Ninety-five years ago, on Sept. 18, 1931, Japan launched an act of aggression in northeast China that marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China, one of the darkest chapters in modern Chinese history. The smoke of war has long dissipated, but the lessons of that history remain relevant. Remembering the September 18 Incident today is not about perpetuating hatred. It is about understanding how militarism once led Japan down the path of aggression, and why any sign of that path being revisited deserves vigilance. History shows that Japanese militarists repeatedly invoked so-called "existential crises" to justify expansion. The occupation of northeast China was presented as necessary for Japan's survival. Now, Japan's incumbent leader has wantonly claimed that a so-called "Taiwan contingency" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, and has even threatened the use of force against China. The gimmick of invoking an "existential crisis" to justify military intervention is reminiscent of the logic once used by Japanese militarists to pursue aggression in the past. In fact, the resurgence of militaristic tendencies in Japan in recent years deserves close attention. After World War II, Japan adopted a pacifist constitution and committed itself to a peaceful path. Yet some forces within Japan have failed to genuinely reflect on the country's history of aggression and have expressed dissatisfaction with the postwar international arrangements. In recent years, Japan has taken a series of steps to expand its military role and capabilities. Japan has significantly increased defense spending, strengthened its military-industrial capabilities, deployed intermediate and long-range missiles and expanded the scope of the Self-Defense Forces' activities. It has also eased restrictions on arms exports and sought to revise its security doctrines. These moves have raised concerns about Japan's departure from its postwar security framework and the principle of an exclusively defense-oriented policy. Japan has become increasingly involved in matters concerning the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea. Under the pretext of building a "free and open" region, it has strengthened security cooperation with other countries and sought to bring external military forces and mechanisms into the Asia-Pacific. Such moves risk increasing confrontation and adding uncertainty that threatens regional peace and stability. At the same time, efforts to distort or downplay wartime history remain a concern. Visits by Japanese politicians to the Yasukuni Shrine, revisions to history textbooks and changes to historical public narratives have drawn criticism for downplaying or distorting Japan's wartime aggression. Such practices can mislead the public and make it more difficult for Japan to face its history and build trust with neighboring countries that suffered from Japan's aggression. The failure of the international community at that time to effectively restrain Japan's aggression offers a lasting lesson: threats to peace must be taken seriously before they become irreversible. For Japan, the choice is ultimately about what kind of role it wants to play in the region. The Japanese people once witnessed their country being transformed into a war machine under militarism and suffered the consequences of war. Recent anti-war protests in Japan have also reflected strong opposition among the public to sliding back to the militarist path. If Japan's policymakers ignore concerns at home and abroad, disregard the concerns of neighboring countries and move away from their international obligations, they will only plunge Japan into an abyss. History moves forward, but its lessons remain. Any attempt to whitewash aggression, deny wartime crimes or revive militarism runs against the hard-won lessons of the past. Remembering Sept. 18 means ensuring that those lessons are not forgotten, and that the tragedies of history are never repeated.■

item.title: China's property market sees major changes in supply and demand: official
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's property market has seen major changes in supply and demand and entered a new phase increasingly centered on existing housing stock, an official said Friday. The share of second-hand home transactions in total housing transactions rose from 27 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2025, and 52 percent in the first eight months of this year, said Zhang Xuetao, an official with the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, at a press conference. A share exceeding 50 percent marks the property market's transition into the new phase, according to Zhang. To adapt to these changes, China is accelerating efforts to foster a new development model for the real estate sector, Zhang said. The country will press ahead with reforms to three key systems governing property development, financing and sales to promote the sector's sound development. In property development, each real estate project will operate through a dedicated project company that is an independent legal entity, while corporate headquarters will be barred from improperly diverting project funds, Zhang said. In property financing, each project will have one lead bank or banking consortium to manage project funds and meet reasonable financing needs, with the bank and project company sharing benefits and risks, Zhang said. In commercial housing sales, China will promote sales of completed homes to allow buyers to "get what they see" and reduce delivery risks, Zhang said, adding that the share of completed homes in total new-home sales by floor area has risen year by year in recent years. Meanwhile, China will strengthen housing support for low-income urban families, new urban residents and young people, providing rental housing or homes for purchase as appropriate to meet basic housing needs, Zhang said. Efforts to foster a new real estate development model have gathered pace this year. In August, authorities deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system and refined regulations on commercial housing sales and property financing as part of broader efforts to chart a new path for real estate development. Data released earlier this week showed narrower year-on-year declines in home prices across major Chinese cities in August, pointing to further signs of stabilization as China continues city-specific policy adjustments, inventory reduction and urban renewal. Meanwhile, overall property transaction volumes have improved, with second-hand home transactions by floor area rising 10.6 percent year on year in the first eight months, while the total floor area of unsold new commercial housing fell 1.1 percent year on year at the end of August, the sixth straight monthly decline. ■

item.title: China releases 60 new wartime archives on Japanese military's "comfort woman" crime
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
CHANGCHUN, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Jilin Provincial Archives in northeast China on Friday released 60 original Japanese military documents from World War II, adding new evidence of Japan's wartime system of forced sexual slavery. The release coincided with the 95th anniversary of the "Sept. 18 Incident." It was on Sept. 18, 1931, when Japanese troops blew up a section of the railway near Shenyang, then under their control, and accused Chinese troops of sabotage as a pretext for subsequent aggression. The new archives came from charred historical remnants left behind after the Japanese Kwantung Army attempted to destroy them during their retreat, according to the Jilin Provincial Archives in Changchun, capital of Jilin Province. The original Japanese military documents shed further light on the systematic and institutionalized sexual violence committed by the Japanese army, powerfully debunking the long-standing lies of Japan's right-wing forces that distort the facts surrounding the "comfort women" issue and attempt to whitewash Japan's war crimes. Previous research has shown that some 400,000 women in Asia were forced to serve as "comfort women" -- sexual slaves for the Japanese army during World War II -- and nearly half of them were Chinese. Lyu Chunyue, an official with the archives, said the archives now has 85 original Japanese military documents documenting the "comfort women" system. The first 25 were released in 2014 and were later included in China's documentary heritage. The 60 newly released documents cover the establishment and authorization of "comfort stations," their daily operation, the recruitment of sex slaves and their brutal treatment, Lyu said. The documents show that "comfort stations" were established and operated under the authority of the Japanese military, with the Japanese Kwantung Army setting up more than 20 such facilities in Northeast China. Some archives show that military approval was required to establish new "comfort stations," and some were located inside Japanese military barracks and were restricted to military personnel. The new archives also include records on the forced recruitment of sex slaves. A 1941 report by a Japanese military unit said that Japanese troops forcibly recruited Korean women when women could not be recruited voluntarily. Other archives showed that "comfort women" were forcibly conscripted to the front lines under Japan's national mobilization law, thoroughly refuting the fallacy that their recruitment was voluntary. The documents also recorded violence against the sex slaves at multiple "comfort stations." "The release of these original archives, irrefutable proof of crimes against humanity committed by Japanese militarism, provides solid historical evidence for defending historical truth and countering historical revisionism," said Su Zhiliang, leading expert for China's bid to list "comfort women" materials on UNESCO Memory of the World Register. ■

item.title: China firmly opposes so-called voluntary restrictions on hybrid vehicle exports to Europe: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China steadfastly opposes the so-called voluntary restrictions on China's hybrid vehicle exports to Europe, as they gravely violate the World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and run counter to market economy rules and the principle of fair competition, a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said on Friday. The spokesperson made the remarks in response to recent media reports that the European Union (EU) wants China to voluntarily restrict exports of hybrid vehicles to Europe, and that China could otherwise face higher tariffs. "These so-called voluntary export restrictions seriously violate WTO rules and run counter to the laws of the market economy and the principle of fair competition. China firmly opposes this," the spokesperson said. "China's position is consistent. Any solution between China and the EU must ensure a balance of interests, comply with WTO rules and their respective domestic laws, and fully accommodate the interests of industries on both sides," the spokesperson added. ■

item.title: China urges Japan to deeply reflect on history of aggression: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China urges Japan to face up to and deeply reflect on its history of aggression, and gain the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community with concrete actions, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a press briefing on Friday. The September 18th Incident 95 years ago marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China. Ninety-five years ago today, Guo said, Japanese militarists launched aggression against China, and they were met by the courageous resistance of the Chinese people, which lifted the curtain of the eastern theater of the World Anti-Fascist War. Noting the September 18th Incident was a war plot long concealed by the Japanese government from the Japanese public, Guo said the vast majority of the Japanese people did not learn the truth until the Tokyo Trials, which opened 80 years ago. The increasingly prevalent historical denialism in Japan is truly troubling, and the danger is self-evident, Guo noted. Denialism not just reflects serious regression in Japan's perception of history, but also indicates alarmingly an organized attempt to turn back the wheel of history with clear political motives, said Guo, adding that the real purpose is to keep the Japanese public from the truth, and clear the path for Japan to escape the straitjacket of the postwar system and rearm itself. Denying the crime of aggression is to challenge historical conclusions and undermine the post-war international order, Guo said, stressing that all countries in the region, including China, must remain highly vigilant, not allow Japanese militarism to resurface, and not let historical tragedies repeat themselves. "We must work together to uphold the outcomes of the World War II victory and jointly safeguard peace", Guo added. ■

item.title: Xi Focus: Steering China's strides toward manufacturing powerhouse
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Defying intense pressures at home and abroad, China's manufacturing sector has forged ahead, accelerating the construction of a modern industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone, and solidifying the foundations for high-quality development. China's manufacturing value-added accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, topping the world for over a decade. That is no accident. It is the result of the insight and leadership of Chinese President Xi Jinping over the past years. As early as 2018, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that China was experiencing a decline in manufacturing's share of the economy that was too fast, and the problem demanded close attention. At a national conference on advanced manufacturing recently held in Beijing, Xi stressed the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone and to reinforce the foundations of the real economy. ANCHORING REAL ECONOMY In May 2025, Xi visited Luoyang Bearing Group in Henan Province. Bearings are the joints of the entire manufacturing body, setting the performance ceiling for high-speed rail, wind turbines and aerospace alike. Standing on the factory floor, Xi reflected on China's industrial journey. "From importing matches, soaps and iron products to becoming the world's largest manufacturing country with the most complete industrial sectors and categories, China has always adhered to the path of developing the real economy, which has proven to be the right path." Over the years, Xi has walked the length and breadth of China's manufacturing landscape, and each stop has reinforced the same conviction that for a country of China's size, developing the real economy is non-negotiable. At Gree Electric Appliances in 2018, he noted that advanced manufacturing is a key component of the real economy and that at no time should economic development become decoupled from the real economy and shift toward the virtual. At Zhengzhou Coal Mining Machinery the following year, he called manufacturing "the foundation of the real economy" and the real economy "the bedrock of the country's development." And at a "little giant" firm, Yangquan Valve, in 2025, Xi emphasized that the real economy should not be neglected, nor should the traditional industries within it. Behind these instructions lies a profound reading of global economic history. International experience shows that manufacturing's share of GDP typically peaks and then declines as industrialization matures. When the decline goes too far, it hollows out industries and leaves an economy vulnerable to risks. Under Xi's strategic vision, the country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) explicitly proposes moving faster to strengthen manufacturing, calling for maintaining a reasonable share of manufacturing in the economy and building a modern industrial system led by advanced manufacturing. The president has also clarified the direction: high-end, intelligent, and green manufacturing. China's manufacturing sector has been remarkably successful. In 2013, China sold just 17,600 new energy vehicles (NEVs), with market penetration at 0.08 percent. By 2025, annual sales had surged to 16.49 million units, with penetration reaching 47.9 percent. In shipbuilding, China had held the top spot globally for 16 consecutive years by 2025, completing 56 percent of the world's ships and holding two-thirds of global orders last year. The same year, China's industrial robot exports grew 48.7 percent over 2024, surpassing imports for the first time and making China a net exporter of industrial robots. BREAKING BOTTLENECKS THROUGH INNOVATION While inspecting Wuhan HGLaser Engineering Co., Ltd. in June 2022, Xi attentively watched a display of innovative achievements in the chip industry and said earnestly: "With our country's further development, it is urgent to address the bottlenecks in core technologies in key fields." For Xi, self-reliance and independent innovation are not slogans -- they are the fundamental guarantee for China's manufacturing to stand firm over the long run. In the spring of 2023, a moment at the "two sessions," the annual meetings of China's top legislature and political advisory body, vividly showcased the confidence of China's manufacturing sector as it strides toward innovation and strength. Shan Zenghai, a deputy from Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group (XCMG), a leading heavy machinery manufacturer, said that the company's 220-tonne all-terrain crane can now be 100 percent domestically produced, during a deliberation of deputies from Jiangsu Province. "What about the chips in the cranes? Are they also homegrown?" Xi inquired. The answer was affirmative. Shan said that XCMG manufactured 91 percent of all components in its products, up from 62 percent previously. Xi commended the company's achievements in making world-class engineering machinery. "We need to upgrade to medium- and high-end manufacturing. This is a hallmark of high-quality development." The Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee has repeatedly dedicated study sessions to frontier technologies. Concrete measures have followed. China has established national manufacturing innovation centers, launched major science and technology projects, rolled out a decade-long action plan for basic research, and focused on full-chain breakthroughs in critical sectors, including integrated circuits and industrial machine tools. In the first half of this year, China's major industrial enterprises produced 279.8 billion integrated circuit units, surging 23.1 percent year on year. POWERING THE WORLD From solar panels harvesting sunlight in Egypt's deserts to China-Europe freight trains carrying equipment across Eurasia, China's manufacturing has become deeply embedded in global supply chains, powering the world with affordable, high-quality products and technologies. "As we further modernize our industrial system, we will provide the world with more and better products made and created in China, and with a Chinese market of a larger scale and stronger demand," Xi said at a meeting in 2023. This pledge is being translated into concrete action. Today, China has fully eliminated market access restrictions for foreign investment in the manufacturing sector. The updated catalog of encouraged foreign investment industries channels foreign capital into advanced manufacturing and other high-end fields, while international standards exchanges in areas such as NEVs and artificial intelligence continue to deepen. As the world's largest manufacturing country, China has built extensive, well-integrated production capacity across a wide range of industrial goods, allowing producers worldwide to access key equipment, components and intermediate goods at lower cost and with greater efficiency. Through technological innovation and intense market competition, China has built the world's largest and most integrated supply chains for the new energy industry. Chinese solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and NEVs have made energy transition more affordable. Attending the BRICS summit in New Delhi last week, Xi proposed five initiatives, including an intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative. He said China stands ready to help fellow BRICS countries build smart factories, develop standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading. Experts noted that Chinese products have won markets with their proven strength, and Chinese manufacturing has built deep confidence with its remarkable resilience. This is a powerful testament to the strategic vision of developing advanced manufacturing, and a vivid display of the broad horizons of innovation-driven progress. ■
